description: We're a team of computer engineers and data scientists looking to put our knowledge into practical projects and gain valuable insights in the process.
summary: Sol Check is an offline-first health monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions. Crew members log vital signs, symptoms, sleep and mood. The app compares each check-in with that astronaut’s own baseline, explains which changes need attention and records follow-up for the onboard Crew Medical Officer. In our simulated Mars mission, Sol Check flags a sustained drop in sleep and mood after two sols in storm shelter and lets the crew prepare an Earth handoff while communications are delayed. We replay Curiosity radiation measurements for environmental context and use Inspiration4 blood counts to show how a change from a personal baseline can fall within a population reference range.
details:
On Sol 43 of a simulated Mars mission, Maya Chen logs 4.5 hours of sleep after two sols in storm shelter. Her recent baseline is 7.5 hours. Sol Check spots a sustained decline in sleep and mood and routes the finding to the onboard Crew Medical Officer. At the scenario’s 20-minute one-way light time, the crew can review the evidence, record a follow-up and prepare a ground briefing from the same device.

Crew members record pulse, blood pressure, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and symptoms. The rule engine looks back 14 sols and requires at least five usable measured sols to calculate a personal baseline. Every finding shows the observations and rule that triggered it. The Crew Medical Officer can acknowledge follow-up tasks and document what happened. The app exports a human-readable briefing or a structured JSON handoff and includes a simulator for delayed ground exchanges.

NASA’s five hazards frame the hazard explorer. The mission timeline overlays 1,220 archived Curiosity RAD measurements, aggregated into 330 hourly medians with gaps preserved, alongside the fictional shelter timeline. The rover data describes the Mars surface environment. The crew and cabin readings, shielding and compartment radiation events are simulated. In a separate retrospective exercise using NASA OSDR’s Inspiration4 study, all 20 day-after-return blood-count values were within the lab’s reference ranges and four crossed the prototype’s personal-change thresholds. The small analysis illustrates what an individual baseline can surface.

We built the app in TypeScript with React and Vite, using Workbox to cache the production web app and Capacitor to package mobile builds. Three.js and Blender support a 3D astronaut for exploring health trends and an ISS-based habitat view for replaying simulated radiation events. Optional camera and microphone checks run on the device. The crew reviews estimates and voice-drafted entries before saving. Ask Sol supports text and hands-free interaction using local records and rules, with speech models for transcription and playback.

Sol Check gives a crew a way to notice change, understand the evidence and coordinate a response when Earth is minutes away. The same record-and-handoff workflow could be evaluated by isolated teams on Earth. Clinical and flight validation are outside the scope of this research prototype.

SI development and runtime disclosure

Team Rocket Engine used OpenAI Codex for the initial offline application, local records, baseline rules and RadLab processing. Google Gemini and Antigravity assisted with camera integration, replay, exports and browser verification. Anthropic Claude assisted with the console interface, 3D viewer and measurement guides. The demo crew and habitat records are synthetic. The Curiosity and Inspiration4 source data come from NASA archives, and the transformations are documented in the repository. On-device models support optional camera estimates, speech recognition and speech synthesis. Health findings and follow-up routing use deterministic rules. Bundled alert audio and spoken replies are synthesized with Piper or Kokoro.
